item.title: Spacewalkers complete space station solar power upgrade
item.description:
Completing a complex upgrade five years in the making, two spacewalking astronauts on Thursday mounted an eighth and final roll-out solar wing on the International Space Station, boosting the lab's power output to compensate for the age-related degradation of its original arrays.
NASA began the power-system upgrade in 2021 when two spacewalkers installed the first ISS roll-out solar array, or IROSA, at the base of one of the original eight wings. Six additional panels were attached during subsequent spacewalks, with the most recent installation carried out last week during a spacewalk by NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk.
Astronaut Anil Menon, anchored to the end of the International Space Station's robot arm, carries the eighth and final set of add-on solar arrays to the far right side of the lab's power truss for installation.
NASA TV
The duo ventured back outside Thursday to install the eighth and final IROSA on the far right end of the station's power truss, beginning the extravehicular activity, or EVA — NASA speak for "spacewalk" — at 8:36 a.m. ET.
The final two IROSAs were delivered to the station aboard a SpaceX Cargo Dragon capsule earlier this month, with each one folded in half and stowed in the ship's unpressurized trunk section. The lab's robot arm mounted both rolled-up blankets on the left side of the station's power truss to await installation.
Attachment and extension of the seventh panel last week was relatively straightforward because the 58-foot-long robot arm could easily carry Menon, holding onto a new IROSA, to its nearby installation point on a fixture at the base of an inboard left-side solar wing.

item.title: Oil prices rebound slightly as Iran claims new attacks on ships
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war: Oil prices fell sharply after the midterm elections, as markets appeared to hope the results might push President Trump toward a deal to end the Iran war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Commercial ships in the region continue coming under attack, however, and hitting sea mines, according to Iranian authorities. As a senior Iranian security official met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin amid uncertainty over Mr. Trump's next move, Moscow warned Russian citizens not to visit Iran, citing the "risk of a new escalation." Oman said Thursday it was still in talks with Iran aimed at creating a system for the nations to jointly control traffic through the vital shipping lanes of the strait, which the Omani foreign ministry said could "end the state of war and prevent renewed confrontations in the region."
New Updates

Putin, Iran's security chief discuss building oil pipeline from Russia to Iran
Russian President Vladimir Putin received Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between their two countries, including a pipeline to import Russian gas.
Speaking to journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy.
"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.

item.title: Mexican judge accused by U.S. of taking bribes in major drug case
item.description:
A Mexican judge has been arrested and accused of accepting $2 million in bribes in exchange for releasing a suspected Canadian drug trafficker from custody, U.S. officials said Thursday.
Luiz Benítez Alcántara was overseeing extradition proceedings in Mexico in 2024 for Canadian citizen Andrew Clark, who was charged in the U.S. with helping to run a billion-dollar drug trafficking group allegedly headed by former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, the Justice Department said in a statement. Benítez is accused of releasing Clark from custody after accepting the bribe payments, according to the statement.
Clark was arrested days after his release and removed to the United States, where he faces drug trafficking and murder charges.
The statement said Benítez, 49, was arrested Sunday in Colombia. He is charged in a nine-count indictment with being an accessory after the fact. It was not immediately known if he has a lawyer.
U.S. officials will request Benítez's extradition from Colombia, the statement said.
Luiz Benítez Alcántara
Department of Justice
"Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the statement.
It's the latest arrest in the U.S. investigation into a multinational drug trafficking network allegedly run by Wedding, who became a top FBI fugitive accused of moving cocaine from Latin America into the United States and orchestrating several killings. Wedding was arrested in Mexico earlier this year and flown to California, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and drug charges.

item.title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights within hours
item.description:
Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act."
British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent.
So far, it remains unclear who, if anyone, is behind any such coordinated action, and no authorities have confirmed a link between any of the threats.
David Kaminski-Morrow, Air Transport Editor with FlightGlobal, declined to speculate on who might be behind the threats this week, but he noted that "we currently live in a time of political aggression in regions including Europe, and it's a pretty effective tactic if someone is looking to cause disruption."
"The cluster of threats seems unusual, but it's hard to determine the extent to which they might be organized," he said, noting that "the publicity alone could spur further threats unrelated to earlier ones."

item.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
item.description:
Actor and comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three other women on Thursday at his trial in London. Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand will be sentenced to prison.
Brand, 51, was initially accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault. On Thursday, he was acquitted of two rape counts and the attempted indecent assault charge.
"You've been convicted of a number of offences including rape," Bennathan told Brand after reading Thursday's verdict, according to CBS News partner BBC. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody."
Brand, who was denied bail and taken into custody, will be sentenced on Monday.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said, according to the Associated Press. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
British comedian and actor Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London on Nov. 5, 2026.
Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty Images
The allegations, made by six women, spanned a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.
A jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days. They found Brand guilty of grabbing a woman's breasts during a party at a bar in London's Soho neighborhood in the summer of 2004, sexually assaulting a woman at London radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005, and raping a woman at his home in Hampstead in 2009.

item.title: U.S. ID's remains of WWII soldier from iconic "Merrill's Marauders"
item.description:
The United States military announced Wednesday that it has identified the remains of a soldier who belonged to the iconic "Merrill's Marauders" unit during World War II, more than 80 years after his disappearance.
Joseph Gala, of Lynn, Massachusetts, was declared killed in action on July 14, 1944, two months after he went missing during a mission in what was then Burma, now Myanmar, according to the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency.
Gala was 21 when he died. Although the circumstances of his death were never recorded, he was last seen advancing with his battalion toward a heavily-fortified Japanese area near the village of Mankrin, the military said.
Gala had fought alongside a volunteer infantry unit that came to be known as "Merrill's Marauders," named after its commander. The battalion was solicited by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to fulfill a "secret and dangerous mission" in the China-Burma-India Theater — the war's so-called "forgotten theater," as the Army described it in a 2016 article. About 3,000 young men volunteered for the mission, and just 200 returned home.
"Those that volunteered had no idea what the mission was going to be," Robert Passanisi, one of troops who did survive, told CBS New York in 2013.
Recalling his unit's 1,000-mile march through the Burmese jungle to disrupt Japanese supply lines, Passanisi added: "It's pretty well-known that nobody else ever did anything as strenuous, as enduring and as difficult in such miserable terrain."
The 5307th Composite Unit (Provisional), also known as "Merrill's Marauders," pictured during World War II.

item.title: Newly found prehistoric "giant rat" species named after princess
item.description:
A giant rodent weighing around 66 pounds roamed what is now southern Thailand 33 to 35 million years ago, scientists said, after identifying a previously unknown species from two fossilized teeth.
The ancient animal, which one geologist on the team called a "giant rat," was among the largest known from the Paleogene period, offering new clues about how early rodents evolved to enormous sizes.
The findings, published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Reports, were based on a molar and an incisor discovered in 2004 at a coal mine in southern Krabi province.
Pannipa Tian, a geologist with Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, who found the incisor, said she initially misidentified the fossil because of its "unusually large size."
"At first, I thought it was a bone. I showed it to my supervisor, who told me it was a giant rat's tooth," Pannipa, 51, told AFP on Thursday.
The cream-colored fossil stood out against the dark coal deposits, while another expedition member found the dark-colored molar the same day.
The Krabi basin has previously yielded fossils of ancient primates, carnivores and hoofed mammals.
But at the time of the discovery, the team lacked sufficient evidence and technology to identify the species.
More than two decades later, researchers from Thailand, France and Canada were able to do so through detailed analysis of the teeth.
The animal weighed around 30 kilograms — an estimated half as much as a large capybara, the world's largest living rodent, they said.

item.title: Ronaldo retires from Portugal national team
item.description:
Lisbon, Portugal — Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.
The announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after a falling out with coach Jorge Jesus.
"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. "I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.
"Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end."
While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League.
Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn't plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team's training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him.
The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing "deep gratitude and immense admiration" for Ronaldo's service to the country.
"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" the federation said.
